newsitem.title: FRANCE: Spanish firm to resume work on Algerian dam.
newsitem.headline: Spanish firm to resume work on Algerian dam.

text.p: Spanish builder Dragados is to resume work, halted three years ago by violence, on Algeria's Beni Haroun dam, the official news agency APS said on Sunday.
The dam, the country's biggest water project, is partly financed by the Saudi Development Fund.

Work on the 795 million cubic metre-capacity dam in the northeastern province of Mila, 280 km (175 miles) from Algeria, was, like dozens of other large water projects, abruptly stopped because of violence blamed by officials on Moslem militants.

Beni Haroun dam will supply drinking water to the eastern provinces of Mila, Constantine, Jijel, Khenchela, Oum el Bouaghi and Batna, and irrigate agricultural projects in the high plains around Constantine.
The dam will also generate power for a hydroelectric plant in Mila.

The announcement that work would resume coincided with a meeting on Sunday between a delegation of Spanish businessmen and Algerians over several joint ventures and investment in small and medium-size businesses covering the pharmaceutical, machinery and agricultural sectors.
The Madrid government has earmarked $400 million loan lines this year to foster economic cooperation with Algeria.

Spain's state secretary in charge of cooperation Fernando Maria Villalonga Campos is due in Algiers to preside with his Algerian counterpart Lahcene Moussaoui over a two-day conference on Monday to boost economic relations.
Algeria bought the equivalent of 9 percent of its overall imports, which totalled $10.7 billion in 1995, from Spain.
Spain was ranked the fourth trader with the North African country with more than $900 million in imports.

Business between the two Mediterranean countries is expected to soar shortly with the opening in November of an Algerian gas pipeline, carrying 8.5 billion cubic metre to Spain via Morocco and the Strait of Gibraltar.
A week ago, German investors led by junior minister Werner Hoyer also visited Algeria. The visits are seen by Algerian officials as a fresh signal of European confidence in Algeria.

An estimated 50,000 people, including more than 100 foreigners, have died in Algeria's violence pitting Moslem guerrillas against the government since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
